desc:
Given a binary search tree with distinct values and two values p and q that both occur in the tree, return the value of their lowest common ancestor: the deepest node that has both p and q in its subtree. A node counts as part of its own subtree, so if p is an ancestor of q the answer is p. It is allowed that p == q.

Tree encoding. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level order. The first entry is the root. After that, the left and right child of every existing node are written in turn, level by level, from left to right. A missing child is written as -1 (node values are never negative, so -1 cannot be confused with a value). Missing nodes have no children listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped. The empty tree is [].

For example, [8,3,10,1,6,-1,14] is the tree whose root 8 has children 3 and 10; node 3 has children 1 and 6; node 10 has no left child and right child 14.

Example 1

tree = [8,3,10,1,6,-1,14,-1,-1,4,7,13], p = 4, q = 7
Output: 6

Example 2

tree = [8,3,10,1,6,-1,14,-1,-1,4,7,13], p = 1, q = 13
Output: 8

Example 3

tree = [8,3,10,1,6,-1,14,-1,-1,4,7,13], p = 3, q = 4
Output: 3
3 is an ancestor of 4.
constraints: 0 ≤ node value ≤ 100,000, all values distinct; the tree is a valid BST
p and q are values that occur in the tree (they may be equal)
hints: For a general binary tree you would have to search both subtrees. What extra information does the BST order give you at every node?
Look at the current node v. If both p and q are smaller than v, they are both in the left subtree. What if both are larger?
Start at the root. Move left while both targets are smaller, move right while both are larger. The first node where they split (or where it equals one of them) is the answer.
editorial: Standing at a node v, the BST order tells you where each target is: smaller values are in the left subtree, larger ones in the right subtree. If both targets are smaller than v the lowest common ancestor is inside the left subtree, so move there. If both are larger, move right. Otherwise one target is on each side (or v is itself one of them), so v has both in its subtree while none of its children does: that is the lowest common ancestor.
The walk goes down one path and never backtracks, so it takes O(h) time after decoding the array in O(n). No recursion is needed, which also avoids stack overflows on path-shaped trees.
